title: Takeaways from #NCTE14 (and why professional conferences are worth it)
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Writing after his first national teachers' conference, NCTE's 2014 annual meeting, Stuart makes a balanced case that professional conferences are worth their cost if teachers and schools approach them deliberately. On the plus side he lists the reboot effect of stepping away from a year's accumulated clutter, hearing admired authors present current work, discovering unknown presenters, and the humbling double realization that one is neither the best nor the worst teacher in the world. Against that he sets information overload, which turns good intentions into few actual changes, and cost, itemizing roughly $900 for a frugal trip and linking expense to the sustainable lifestyle teachers need to avoid burnout. His remedies are realistic expectations, advance networking, seeking outside funding and a concise takeaway list. Through Steven Pressfield's The War of Art he names the conference's main lesson: nothing replaces simply doing the work. He closes by addressing school leaders, arguing that the fairness problem of limited budgets should be solved by rotation, as one Idaho district does every five years, rather than by sending no one.
points: Stuart's argument is conditional: conferences refresh and humble teachers, but only a prioritized takeaway list converts the flood of sessions into actual classroom change.
He ties conference cost directly to teacher sustainability, itemizing a frugal $900 trip and arguing that draining teachers' finances undermines the lifestyle they need to avoid burnout.
A key benefit he names is calibration - learning that you are neither the best nor the worst teacher in the world - which most teachers need on the second count.
Via Pressfield's The War of Art, his chief takeaway is that nothing replaces the power of simply doing the work of teaching.

For school leaders he offers a specific policy model - funding each teacher's national conference on a rotating five-year cycle - and rejects sending no one simply because it is the easiest fair option.
quotes: Attending a conference like #NCTE14 is invigorating and refreshing. It's like rebooting a computer that's been left on since September with 40 tabs open.

Conferences are kind of like the Internet in that there is too much information. Without some kind of prioritized, simplified takeaway list (hence my video below), you'll have great intentions of tweaking all kinds of things in your classroom but will actually tweak very few.

They are expensive. This is bad because teachers need to develop sustainable lifestyles if they are to flourish in their jobs and avoid permanent burnout — ridding them of scrilla is not a great way to facilitate a sustainable lifestyle.
Go with realistic expectations. You're likely to get all the helpful stuff in the list above, but you're not going to find answers to every problem that ails you.

One woman I spoke to teaches English and art at a small high school in Idaho; her district sends teachers to national conferences on a rotating, every-five-years basis. This is smart. Folks who want to go every year can pay their own way most years, but every five years they get a free trip to develop themselves as professionals.

After all, it is expensive sending folks to conferences, and unless you prepare, attend, and reflect well, there's bound to be a lot of wasted district money in sending every teacher who asks every year.
